rows.verified: HSE lead guidance covers health effects, employer actions, higher-risk situations, significant exposure, case studies and frequently asked questions.
Lead may be encountered in roof flashings and in older paint or pipework during construction and refurbishment.
The Control of Lead at Work Regulations 2002 require employers to protect employees from lead exposure risks.
Employers should identify tasks that use lead or generate lead dust or fume and assess whether significant exposure is expected.
Workers need suitable information and training and must use protective equipment in accordance with instructions.
Lead-contaminated work areas should be kept clean, and lead waste should be removed through controlled arrangements.
Eating and drinking should be restricted to designated areas free from lead contamination, supported by high standards of personal hygiene.
Medical surveillance under the Control of Lead at Work Regulations is supported by HSE appointed-doctor guidance.
Lead risk depends on chemical form, concentration, task, dust or fume generation, exposure route, duration, controls and worker susceptibility.
Lead guidance is task-, material-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
Employers must manage ionising-radiation risks to protect workers and members of the public.
Ionising radiation includes X-rays, gamma rays and particulate radiation from radioactive substances or radiation-generating equipment.
Ionising-radiation work occurs in manufacturing, food production, construction, engineering, oil and gas, medical, veterinary, dental, education and research settings.
Before most work with ionising radiation, employers must notify HSE or apply for registration or consent according to the risk tier.
Exposure must be restricted as low as reasonably practicable, with engineering controls and design features prioritised before safe systems and PPE.
Risk assessment should estimate potential doses and determine whether personal monitoring or classification of workers is needed.
Specified overexposure events, equipment malfunctions and losses, thefts or releases of radioactive material may require reporting to HSE.
Radiation-emergency duties may apply where an incident could expose a member of the public above specified levels.
Ionising-radiation risk depends on radiation type, activity or generator output, geometry, shielding, time, distance, containment and emergency conditions.
Ionising-radiation evidence is source-, task-, dose-, facility- and person-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health probability.
